turn_text: We're very excited to have with us today, Congressman Jake Okinglos. Congressman Okinglos represents the 4th district in Massachusetts, all the way from Brookline, Newton, down to Fall River. First of all, thank you for your time, Congressman, and thank you for spending some time with the Greek audience here in Massachusetts.

Let's obviously we're in an election year, you do run unopposed. What do you see is the biggest issue locally? You represent a district with very wide range of economics and the social different neighborhoods. What do you see locally is the biggest issue in Massachusetts?

Two things. First, the cost of living. It is too expensive to heat your home, to fill up your gas tank, to get groceries, to pay for medicines, costs for almost everything across the economy have gone up. In Massachusetts, in particular, housing is really driving inflation. Massachusetts has an affordable housing crisis. Since my time as a city councilor and Newton on the land use committee now up to my service as vice chair of the financial services committee which has jurisdiction over housing. I have constantly been advocating for liberalizing our zoning rules so we can build more multi-family housing in Massachusetts. And also for putting more resources behind public-private partnerships to make more housing permanently affordable. Massachusetts needs to build hundreds of thousands of new units of housing until, and unless we do that, housing costs are going to continue to price people out of living in the base state, make it too hard for young people to get started at home, make it too hard for older Americans to downsize into the kinds of amenity-rich apartments that they're looking for, we need to build more housing in this state. Number two is largely due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. We've seen energy prices skyrocket throughout the United States, but particularly in Massachusetts for more than any other state in the union is highly sensitive to natural gas prices in Europe. We're actually really in Energy Island here in Massachusetts. We import much of our LNG, and that LNG that we import is competing for the spot price in Europe. So we're seating home-eating bills this winter, potentially going up by almost $500 over the course of the winter for many of my constituents in the South Coast. It'd be about $200 for many bank constituents closer to Boston. That's going to be very painful for people. I'm acutely aware of that. And it underscores why it's so critical for Massachusetts and the nation to achieve clean energy independence. We need to be in charge of our own destiny. We need to make energy too cheap to meter. And the thing is we know how to do that. We've seen with offshore wind, with geothermal, with solar. We can make investments as we have this Congress to To generate clean renewable energy that can be too cheap to meter and that can provide energy security for residents here in the Bay State. Now, that is our long term aspiration. We know it's not going to happen overnight. We continue to rely on natural gas in the short term and we need to. plus up our low-income heating program and our Northeast home heating oil supplies so that we can help people here in the short term. So I'm very aware that cost of living from making situations is a real struggle right now. There are some things that we're doing to prevent and mitigate that in the short term like capping out of pocket costs for medicines for people on Medicare, but the trade-offs remain. The second big thing besides for cost of living is a lot of anxiety about the increasing extremism of We have seen with women's reproductive rights. We have seen with election denial. We have seen with science denial around climate change and vaccinations that the dominant faction within the GOP, the Trump, MAGA crowd really are uninterested in shared facts and in supporting our common democracy. And they are really interested more in an authoritarian approach to governance that is divorced from from facts, data, and from our constitutional norms. And it's scary. It is unnerving to work with these people in Congress. And it's unnerving, I know, from my constituents who are reading headlines that make them feel like they don't recognize their country anymore. And that's what's on the ballot in a few weeks now, is a speaker of the House, potentially Kevin McCarthy, whose first phone call would beat a Donald Trump to ask what to do next. That's not really acceptable. And so we need to beat back this authoritarian wing of the GOP and restore the conventions and the laws that I think until 2016 many Americans took for granted.

turn_text: Well, thank you for that. I'm sure we were very impressed and proud of that, but listening from you, that impression, I'm sure that you were not the only member in Congress who thought that. I was not. I want to hear your views about Ukraine and the war in Ukraine. Again, as a member of Congress, you do have a very heavy saying on the foreign policy, the aid we're giving to Ukraine. Give us a sense after we have been over six months now, Russia looks like it's retreating. In the beginning, it was the fear of Russia winning. Now, it seems to me it's the fear of Russia losing and what they could do in a situation that they're back in a corner.

I have worked across the aisle to champion bipartisan support in Congress for the strategic defeat of Russia in Ukraine. The United States needs to lead the world in upholding the post-war rules-based order, and I think Greeks can well appreciate how important that post-World War II rules-based order has been for spreading peace and prosperity ever more widely. And we also need to send a message to the authoritarian regime in Moscow and Beijing as well that might does not make right. And the United States is going to stand with freedom and democracy when it is under duress. I think exceeding almost everybody's expectations, the Ukrainians have fought with a courage and an ingenuity that has got the Russians back on their heels. We need to continue to provide sustained military and material support to the Ukrainian fighters so that they can continue their advance in the northeast as well as the south. We also need to provide humanitarian and economic aid so they can keep their economy going and prevent the worst suffering. And we've got to continue to strangle the Russian economy with central bank, commercial, and most importantly, energy sanctions. That's the trifecta. We've already done the central bank sanctions. They were effective. The commercial sanctions are going to bite increasingly hard in 2023 and 2024 in preventing the Russian avionics and maritime and military and semiconductor and electronics industries from being able to replenish their stock. But the energy sanctions are the most important right now because The Kremlin has been funding this illegal war with the hard currency of their oil and natural gas shipments, particularly oil. For that reason, I've led a bipartisan letter to Treasury in support of the G7's proposed price caps on Russian oil, which would do two things. I won't get into all the mechanics of it, but basically it would lower prices for Western energy consumers, while also depriving the Kremlin of market rate hard currency for their oil shipments. It's a win-win requires a strong diplomatic international effort. If we can pull it off, it would be a tremendous blow for Ukraine in favor of their defense of the homeland. We need to stand with Ukraine for this winter coming up. It's going to be a hard winter. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. It's going to be a hard winter for the Ukrainians who are fighting on the front lines. It's going to be a hard winter for the Europeans who are dealing with exorbitantly high energy bills. And it's going to be a tough winter also, potentially for the United States. We're also going to face higher energy bills and potentially higher food bills and a pinching economy. But there are some things worth sacrificing for, and the free world is one of them.
